questions.q: What does it mean for a SOQL query to be 'selective'?
options: It returns fewer than 100 rows no matter the object size
It uses exactly one WHERE condition
Its filter narrows the result set down to a small enough fraction of the object's rows that the optimizer chooses to use an index
It avoids using any relationship fields
questions.explain: Selectivity is about the proportion of the object's total rows a filter matches, relative to documented percentage thresholds, not an absolute row count.

questions.q: What is the standard-index selectivity threshold for the first 1,000,000 records of an object?
options: Fewer than 30% of records
Fewer than 10% of records
Fewer than 50% of records
Exactly 15% of records
questions.explain: A standard-indexed filter is selective if it matches fewer than 30% of the first million targeted records (15% beyond that).

questions.q: Why is the custom-index selectivity threshold stricter (lower percentage) than the standard-index threshold?
options: There is no difference between the two thresholds
Custom indexes are actually more efficient than standard indexes, so they need fewer matching records to be useful
Custom indexes only apply to picklist fields
Custom indexes are documented with a tighter bar — under 10% of the first million records, versus 30% for a standard index
questions.explain: Salesforce documents a stricter threshold for custom indexes (under 10%/5%) compared to standard indexes (under 30%/15%).

questions.q: Which of these is true about index usage and object growth over time?
options: Selectivity thresholds are fixed row counts, not percentages, so growth never changes selectivity
A filter that was selective when a table was small can become unselective as the table grows, with no change to the query itself
Once a query is selective, it remains selective forever regardless of data growth
Index usage is determined only by the query's syntax, never by data volume
questions.explain: Because thresholds are percentage-based relative to object size, the same absolute filter can shift from selective to unselective purely as a result of the object growing.

questions.q: Which of these operators generally CANNOT use an index, even on an indexed field?
options: IN with a short list of values
= (equals) on an indexed field
!= (not equals) and a leading-wildcard LIKE '%term'
A simple AND combining two indexed equality filters
questions.explain: Negative filters like != and leading-wildcard LIKE patterns generally can't use an index, because they don't narrow results down the way an index lookup requires.
